lesson.intro: After arrays and hash maps, trees are the most common interview topic. Nearly every tree problem uses one of two moves: recurse into the children and combine answers, or walk level by level with a queue. Add the BST rule and why shape decides speed.
objectives: Write recursive tree functions from what each call needs
Produce pre, in, post and level order and pick the right one
Search, validate and find common ancestors in a BST in O(h)
Explain how height drives cost in balanced and degenerate trees

sections.title: Tree vocabulary and how trees arrive
sections.key: A binary tree is nodes joined by edges with no cycles, each with at most a left and a right child; interviews hand you its root as a `TreeNode`.
sections.body:
Your computer's folders form a tree. A **tree** is a set of nodes joined by edges, with no cycles and exactly one path between any two nodes. The top node is the **root**. In a **binary tree** each node has at most two children, `left` and `right`.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Watch out: many problems' "maximum depth" counts **nodes**, not edges, so a single node has maximum depth 1. Check the examples.

Examples write a tree as a **level-order array**: values row by row, left to right, `null` for a missing child. Children of a missing node are not written, and trailing nulls are dropped. In `[3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]`, 3 is the root with children 9 and 20; 9 has none; 20 has 15 and 7.

visual.title: Reading a level-order array
visual.caption: `[3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]`. Height 2, counted in edges; maximum depth 3, counted in nodes.

visual.title: Words interviewers use
rows: The only node with no parent
Edges from the root down to it; the root has depth 0
Edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf
A node plus all its descendants. It is a tree itself, which is why recursion fits
The family words mean what you expect

sections.code:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

root = TreeNode(3, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))
print(root.right.left.val)   # 15
sections.pitfall: Mixing up height in edges with depth in nodes gives answers that are off by one. Check the examples: if a single node is expected to return 1, the problem counts nodes.

check.question: In the tree written as `[1, 2, 3, null, 4]`, where is the node 4?
choices: It is the left child of 3
It is the left child of 2
It is a third child of the root
It is the right child of 2
check.explanation: After the root, entries come in pairs: (2, 3) are the root's children, then (null, 4) are 2's children. So 2 has no left child and 4 as its right child. 3's children would come next, and the array ends before them.

sections.title: Recursion on trees: ask your children
sections.key: Most tree functions have three parts: a base case for the empty tree, recursive calls on left and right that you trust, and a step that combines their answers.
sections.body:
Want the longest chain of command below you? Ask each direct report for theirs, take the bigger answer and add one. Each report does the same.

- **Base case:** the answer for an empty tree (`None`): 0, `True`, an empty list.
- **Recurse:** call on `node.left` and `node.right`, and trust each answer: the "leap of faith".
- **Combine:** build this node's answer from the two child answers and `node.val`.

[[visual]]

**Same tree:** two empty trees are equal, one empty tree is not, otherwise the values and both subtree pairs must match. **Invert:** invert both subtrees and swap them.

No call looks at its grandchildren: if you write `node.left.left`, let the recursion do it. Each node is visited once, O(n) time. The call stack is O(h): O(log n) when balanced, O(n) for a chain.

visual.title: Maximum depth, computed bottom up
visual.caption: Each node combines what its two children report; an empty child reports 0.

sections.pitfall: Reading `node.left.val` before checking that `node.left` exists crashes on leaves. Put the `None` check first, as the base case, and let the recursive calls deal with missing children.

activity.title: Count the leaves
activity.prompt: Write `count_leaves(node)` with the same three parts: a base case for None, a case for a node with no children, and a combine step that adds the counts from both subtrees. The tree has 3 leaves (9, 15 and 7), so the program should print `3 3`.

props.code:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

#          3
#         / \
#        9   20
#           /  \
#          15   7
root = TreeNode(3, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))

def max_depth(node):
    if node is None:
        return 0
    return 1 + max(max_depth(node.left), max_depth(node.right))

def count_leaves(node):
    # Base case: an empty tree has no leaves.
    # A node with no children is exactly one leaf.
    # Otherwise, add up the leaves of the two subtrees.
    return 0   # replace this

print(max_depth(root), count_leaves(root))
props.task: Finish count_leaves so the program prints 3 3.

check.question: What extra space does `max_depth` use on a tree of n nodes in which every node has only a right child?
choices: O(1), because no data structure is created
O(log n), because it is a binary tree
O(n), because the call stack grows as deep as the tree
O(n^2), because each call copies the path above it
check.explanation: Every recursive call waits on the stack until its child returns. In a chain of n nodes the calls nest n deep, so the stack holds O(n) frames. O(log n) only applies when the tree is balanced.

sections.title: Depth-first orders: pre, in and post
sections.key: Preorder does a node's work before its children, inorder between them, postorder after them; inorder visits a BST in sorted order.
sections.body:
A recursive visit can do its own work before the children, between them, or after them. Those are the three depth-first orders, and each fits different jobs.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

All three are **depth-first search** (DFS): go as deep as possible before backing up. Interviewers sometimes ask for an iterative version with an explicit stack. Iterative inorder is worth memorizing: go left as far as you can, pushing each node; pop one and visit it; then turn to its right subtree.

Quick check: the root comes first in preorder, last in postorder, and between its two subtrees in inorder.

visual.title: Three orders on that tree
rows: Copying or serializing; passing information down, such as the path so far
Sorted order on a BST, kth smallest
Answers built from the children: heights, sizes, balance, deleting a tree

sections.code:
def preorder(node, out):
    if node:
        out.append(node.val)      # node first
        preorder(node.left, out)
        preorder(node.right, out)

def postorder(node, out):
    if node:
        postorder(node.left, out)
        postorder(node.right, out)
        out.append(node.val)      # node last

def inorder_iterative(root):
    out, stack, curr = [], [], root
    while curr or stack:
        while curr:               # go left as far as possible
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()        # visit
        out.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.right         # then the right subtree
    return out

root = TreeNode(4, TreeNode(2, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(3)),
                TreeNode(6, None, TreeNode(7)))
print(inorder_iterative(root))    # [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7]
sections.tip: If a node needs information from its children, think postorder. If it needs information from its ancestors, think preorder with an extra parameter that carries it down.
sections.pitfall: Python's default recursion limit is about 1000 frames. A degenerate tree with 5,000 nodes makes recursive DFS raise RecursionError; switch to an explicit stack, or raise the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit` if you must.

check.question: You need the 3rd smallest value in a binary search tree. Which traversal produces values in the order you need?
choices: Preorder
Inorder
Postorder
Level order
check.explanation: Inorder visits the left subtree (all smaller values), then the node, then the right subtree (all larger values), so a BST comes out sorted. Stop after the 3rd value. Preorder and postorder follow the tree's shape, not the value order.

sections.title: Breadth-first: one level at a time
sections.key: Level order uses a queue: save its size at the start of each level, pop exactly that many nodes, and push their children to form the next level.
sections.body:
An org chart printed level by level is **level order traversal**: breadth-first search (BFS) with a queue instead of recursion.

Put the root in a queue. While it is not empty, save `size = len(queue)`, the number of nodes on this level. Pop that many, record them and push their children. The queue mixes the end of one level with the start of the next, so the saved size marks the boundary.

[[visual]]

One template answers many questions:

[[visual 2]]

Each node enters and leaves once: O(n) time, O(w) space for maximum width w. Use `collections.deque`, since `list.pop(0)` is O(n). JavaScript has no deque, so a common style builds each next level as a fresh array.

visual.title: Level order on the example tree
visual.caption: Result: `[[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]`.

visual.title: One template, many answers
rows: Stop at the first level holding a leaf; DFS would have to explore every branch

sections.pitfall: Putting `None` into the queue (from an empty root or a missing child) leads to `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'val'`. Handle the empty tree first and only enqueue children that exist.

activity.title: Level order traversal
activity.prompt: Use the queue and the size-of-the-level trick. Before submitting, run it in your head on an empty tree and on a tree that leans entirely to one side.

check.question: Why does the level order code save `size = len(queue)` before the inner loop?
choices: len(queue) is slow, so it is computed only once
It stops the root from being visited twice
deque has no way to check whether it is empty
The queue mixes the end of one level with the start of the next, and the size marks where this level ends
check.explanation: As you pop nodes from the current level you push their children, so the queue soon contains two levels at once. Popping exactly size nodes processes the current level and nothing more. len on a deque is O(1), so speed is not the reason.

sections.title: Binary search trees: the ordering rule
sections.key: In a BST every value in a node's left subtree is smaller and every value in its right subtree is larger, so search walks one path in O(h).
sections.body:
Like a paper dictionary, a **binary search tree** (BST) lets you skip most entries. The **BST property** holds at every node and covers whole subtrees, not just children. (No duplicates here.)

Search: equal, found; smaller, go left; larger, go right. Each step discards a subtree, so search, insert and delete cost O(h).

**Validate a BST** with bounds, not parent and child checks:

[[visual]]

Each node must lie strictly between a `low` and a `high` inherited from its ancestors. Going left, the node's value becomes `high`; going right, `low`. A strictly increasing inorder walk also works.

**Lowest common ancestor** (LCA): the deepest node with both p and q in its subtree, where a node counts as its own ancestor. From the root, go left if both are smaller, right if both are larger; otherwise they split here.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Fooling the parent and child check
visual.caption: Every parent and child pair looks fine, but 3 sits in 5's right subtree. Bounds catch it: 3 must lie between 5 and 6.

visual.title: Lowest common ancestors
visual.caption: LCA of 2 and 8 is 6 (they split at the root). LCA of 2 and 4 is 2 (an ancestor of itself). LCA of 3 and 5 is 4.

sections.pitfall: Validating a BST by comparing each node only with its direct children misses violations further down. Pass the allowed (low, high) range down the recursion instead.

activity.title: Search and traverse a BST
activity.prompt: Search for 60 and count how many nodes you compare against. Then run the in-order traversal and confirm it comes out sorted. Finally, predict where 65 will land before you insert it.

check.question: Which tree breaks the BST property even though every node is greater than its left child and less than its right child?
check.explanation: In [10, 5, 15, null, null, 6, 20], 6 is the left child of 15, which looks fine locally, but 6 lives in 10's right subtree and is smaller than 10. The other trees respect every ancestor's bound.

sections.title: Balanced versus degenerate: shape decides speed
sections.key: Every BST operation costs O(h): about log2(n) levels when the tree is balanced, but n - 1 when sorted input turns it into a chain.
sections.body:
Insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in that order and each value becomes the right child of the one before: a linked list in a tree costume. The order 3, 1, 4, 2, 5 gives height 2.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

- **Balanced:** height near log2(n). A million nodes means about 20 levels.
- **Degenerate** (skewed): height n - 1, no better than scanning a list.

**Self-balancing** BSTs, such as AVL and red-black trees, make small restructurings called rotations on insert and delete to keep the height O(log n). Java's `TreeMap` and C++'s `std::map` are usually red-black trees. You will not code rotations in an interview.

**Height-balanced:** subtree heights differ by at most 1 at every node. One postorder pass returns each height, or -1 once anything is unbalanced: O(n), since no height is computed twice.
sections.deeper:
**Ordered data in Python.** Python has no built-in balanced BST. Use a dict for lookups, `bisect` on a sorted list for modest ordered data, or the third-party `sortedcontainers` package. Database indexes use B-trees, a cousin of the BST with many keys per node, so each level fans out widely and the tree stays shallow on disk.

**Why the naive balance check is slow.** Calling a separate height function at every node measures the same subtrees again and again: O(n log n) on a balanced tree instead of O(n). Returning -1 as a sentinel lets one pass carry both the height and the verdict.
sections.pitfall: Saying "BST search is O(log n)" without the word balanced. The honest answer is O(h): O(log n) when the tree is balanced, O(n) in the worst case.

check.question: You insert 10,000 keys in sorted order into a plain BST that never rebalances. How many comparisons can a search for the largest key take?
choices: About 14
About 10,000
About 100
Exactly 1
check.explanation: Sorted inserts build a chain, so the largest key sits at the bottom of a path of 10,000 nodes. About 14 (log2 of 10,000) is what a balanced tree would give, and that is exactly what self-balancing trees guarantee.

sections.title: Practice: choosing the right tree approach
sections.key: Match the wording to an approach: combine child answers, compare two trees, BFS by level, inorder or bounds for a BST, walk one BST path, or carry a path down.
sections.body:
[[visual]]

Before you code, answer out loud:

- What does my function return for an empty tree?
- What does each call need from its children, or pass down to them?
- Is this a BST or just a binary tree? Value shortcuts only work on a BST.
- Time and space? Usually O(n) time, O(h) space for DFS and O(w) for BFS.

Then test three tiny trees: empty, a single node, and a lopsided chain of three. Lopsided trees catch most bugs, because one child is always missing.

**Diameter** (the longest path between any two nodes, in edges) is a classic: one postorder pass returns heights and updates a best `left + right`.

visual.title: Problem wording to approach
rows: Recursion over two trees, comparing node pairs
BFS with a queue and the level-size trick
Inorder, or (low, high) bounds passed down
Walk one path by comparing values: O(h)
Preorder DFS carrying the path so far

activity.title: Validate a binary search tree
activity.prompt: Use the (low, high) bounds idea. Before submitting, trace your code on [5, 1, 6, null, null, 3, 7], the tree that fools the parent and child check.

check.question: A problem asks for the smallest depth at which any leaf appears, in a huge and very wide tree. Which approach can stop earliest?
choices: Postorder DFS computing the minimum depth of every subtree
Inorder traversal collecting the depth of every leaf
BFS level by level, returning at the first leaf it meets
Sorting all the leaves by depth
check.explanation: BFS visits the tree in order of depth, so the first leaf it pops is at the minimum depth and it can return immediately. DFS-based approaches must explore every branch before they can be sure.

keyTerms.definition: The top node of a tree, the only node with no parent.
Depth: edges from the root down to a node. Height: edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. Maximum depth problems often count nodes instead.
A binary tree where every value in a node's left subtree is smaller and every value in its right subtree is larger.
Depth-first order visiting a node before its children: node, left, right.
Depth-first order visiting left subtree, node, right subtree. Produces sorted output on a BST.
Depth-first order visiting both children before the node, used when a node needs its children's answers.
Breadth-first traversal that visits the tree row by row using a queue.
A tree whose height stays O(log n), so searches and updates take O(log n) steps.
A tree where each node has one child, so its height is n - 1 and operations take O(n).
The deepest node that has both given nodes in its subtree, where a node counts as its own ancestor.

summary: Most tree problems: handle the empty tree, trust the calls on left and right, combine.
Preorder passes information down, postorder combines children, inorder sorts a BST.
BFS with a queue and the level-size trick handles anything described by levels.
Validate a BST with (low, high) bounds, not parent and child checks.
BST operations cost O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why checking each node against only its two children is not enough to prove a tree is a valid binary search tree, and how passing a range of allowed values down the tree fixes it.

questions.question: How many leaves does the tree `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, 6]` have?
questions.explanation: The root 1 has children 2 and 3. Node 2 has children 4 and 5; node 3 has only a right child, 6. The nodes with no children are 4, 5 and 6.

questions.question: What is the height, counted in edges, of the tree `[1, 2, null, 3, null, 4]`?
questions.explanation: Node 2 is 1's left child, 3 is 2's left child and 4 is 3's left child, so the tree is a chain 1 - 2 - 3 - 4. A chain of 4 nodes has 3 edges. Its maximum depth counted in nodes would be 4.

questions.question: Match each term with its meaning.

pairs.right: The only node with no parent
Number of edges from the root down to it
A node plus all of its descendants

questions.explanation: Depth counts edges from the root down to a node, so the root has depth 0. A subtree is any node together with everything below it, which is why recursion fits trees.

questions.question: Which level-order array describes this tree?
choices: [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4]
questions.explanation: The root's children are 2 and 3. Then come 2's children: none on the left, 4 on the right, written as null, 4. The array [1, 2, 3, 4] would make 4 the left child of 2.

questions.question: Put the parts of one call of a recursive tree function in the order they run.
items: Return the base case value if the node is None
Call the function on the left child
Call the function on the right child
Combine the two child results with the node's value and return
questions.explanation: The base case comes first so that missing children are handled before anything reads them. Then the function recurses into both children and combines their answers with its own value.

questions.question: Complete `count_nodes` so it returns the number of nodes in the tree.
choices: return count_nodes(node.left) + count_nodes(node.right)
return 1 + max(count_nodes(node.left), count_nodes(node.right))
return 1 + count_nodes(node.left) + count_nodes(node.right)
return count_nodes(node.left.left) + count_nodes(node.right.right)
questions.explanation: Each node counts itself (the 1) plus everything in both subtrees. Using max would compute the depth instead, and leaving out the 1 would always return 0.

questions.question: This is meant to mirror a tree, but the result has the wrong shape. Why?
choices: node.left is overwritten before the old left subtree is used, so it is lost
The base case should return node instead of None
Inverting must happen before the recursive calls, in preorder
Recursion cannot modify a tree, so a queue is required
questions.explanation: The first assignment replaces node.left with the inverted right subtree, so the original left subtree is lost. The second line inverts that same subtree back and stores it on the right, so both children end up pointing at one subtree. Compute both results before assigning, for example with a tuple assignment.

questions.question: What does `mystery` return for the tree `[5, 3, 8, 1, null, null, 2]`?
questions.explanation: mystery adds a node's value to the totals of both subtrees, so it sums every value: 5 + 3 + 8 + 1 + 2 = 19. Node 1 is 3's left child and 2 is 8's right child.

questions.question: `is_same_tree(p, q)` compares trees with n and m nodes. What is its worst-case time?
choices: O(n * m)
O(n + m), since every node of both trees is visited
O(log n)
O(min(n, m)), since it stops at the first difference
questions.explanation: It only recurses into positions where both trees have a node, and it stops at the first difference, so it examines at most min(n, m) pairs. O(n + m) overstates it: the extra nodes of the bigger tree are never visited.

questions.question: What is the preorder traversal of `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`? List the values separated by commas.
questions.explanation: Preorder visits the node, then its whole left subtree, then its right subtree: 1, then 2 with its children 4 and 5, then 3.

questions.question: What is the postorder traversal of `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`?
questions.explanation: Postorder finishes both subtrees before the node: 4 and 5 before 2, then 3, and the root 1 last. 4, 2, 5, 1, 3 is inorder and 1, 2, 4, 5, 3 is preorder.

questions.question: Match each task with the traversal that fits it best.

pairs.left: Print a BST's values in sorted order
Compute the height of every subtree
Copy a tree, creating each parent before its children
Print the tree one row at a time

questions.explanation: Inorder sorts a BST, postorder has children's answers ready before the parent, preorder handles a parent before its children, and level order goes row by row.

questions.question: `inorder_iterative` returns an empty list for every tree. What is wrong?
choices: curr = curr.right should be curr = curr.left
The outer loop should be while curr or stack, because the stack starts empty
out.append must come before stack.pop()
The inner loop should push curr.right
questions.explanation: The stack starts empty, so `while stack` is false immediately and the loop never runs. The condition must be `while curr or stack`, because at the start the work is in curr, not on the stack.

questions.question: Which data structure drives level order traversal?
choices: A stack (last in, first out)
A hash set
A queue (first in, first out)
A min-heap
questions.explanation: A queue hands nodes back in the order they were added, so a whole level is processed before the next one. A stack would give a depth-first order.

questions.question: What does `level_order` return for `[1, 2, 3, null, 4, null, 5]`? Type it as a Python list of lists.
questions.explanation: Node 2 has only a right child, 4, and node 3 has only a right child, 5. Levels: [1], then [2, 3], then [4, 5].

questions.question: This JavaScript level order builds each level as a fresh array instead of using a queue. What goes in the blank?
choices: next = level
level = next
levels.push(next)
level.push(...next)
questions.explanation: After collecting the children of every node on this level into next, next becomes the level to process. Pushing next into level would make the loop run forever, and pushing it into levels would record node objects instead of values.

questions.question: The right side view lists the node you would see at the right edge of each level, from top to bottom. How do you get it from the level order template?
choices: Record the last node popped on each level
Record the first node popped on each level
Follow right children from the root until there are none
Record node.right.val for every node that has a right child
questions.explanation: The last node popped on each level is the rightmost one, even when it is a left child (for example when its parent has no right child). Following only right children misses those nodes.

questions.question: Why is `queue.pop(0)` on a Python list a poor choice for BFS on a large tree?
choices: It removes the last element, not the first
It shifts every remaining element, so each pop is O(n)
Lists cannot hold TreeNode objects
It raises an error when the list has a single item
questions.explanation: Removing the first item shifts every remaining item one place left, so each pop is O(n) and the traversal can degrade to O(n^2). deque.popleft() is O(1).

questions.question: In a BST you are searching for 7 and the current node holds 10. Where do you go next?
choices: Right, because 7 might be a right child
Both subtrees, because 7 could be anywhere
Left, because all smaller values are in the left subtree
Back to the parent
questions.explanation: Everything smaller than 10 lives in its left subtree, so 7 can only be there. Searching both subtrees would throw away the whole advantage of a BST.

questions.question: Which of these level-order arrays are valid BSTs? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: [8, 4, 12, 2, 9, 10, 14] fails because 9 is in 8's left subtree. [5, 3, 7, null, null, 4, 9] fails because 4 is in 5's right subtree. In [5, 3, 7, null, 4], 4 is 3's right child and still less than 5, so it is fine.

questions.question: Which input makes this `is_valid_bst` return True even though the tree is not a BST?
questions.explanation: The function only compares each node with its direct children. In [10, 5, 15, null, null, 6, 20], 6 is a fine left child of 15 but sits in 10's right subtree, which the local checks never notice. The other inputs are caught by a parent and child comparison.

questions.question: Using `lca_bst` on the tree `[6, 2, 8, 0, 4, 7, 9, null, null, 3, 5]` from this section, what is the lowest common ancestor of 3 and 0?
questions.explanation: At 6 both values are smaller, so go left to 2. At 2, 0 is smaller and 3 is larger, so the paths split and 2 is the answer.
questions.concept: lowest common ancestor in a BST

questions.question: Why can't `lca_bst` be used on an ordinary binary tree that is not a BST?
choices: Comparing values only tells you where a value lives when the BST property holds
Ordinary binary trees can have more than two children
It would take O(n^2) time on an ordinary tree
Ordinary binary trees have no root node
questions.explanation: It chooses left or right by comparing values, and that comparison only tells you where a value lives when the BST property holds. For a general binary tree you need a full DFS that reports whether each subtree contains p or q.

questions.question: You build a BST by inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in that order. What is its height in edges?
questions.explanation: Each value is larger than all earlier ones, so each becomes the right child of the previous node. Seven nodes in a chain have 6 edges. A balanced tree of 7 nodes would have height 2.

questions.question: Which insertion order of 1 through 7 produces a perfectly balanced BST?
questions.explanation: Inserting the middle value first (4), then the middles of each half (2 and 6), then the rest fills every level. Sorted or reverse-sorted orders build chains, and 4, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 hangs a chain on each side of 4, giving height 3.

questions.question: Why is `check_height` (the version that returns -1 for unbalanced) O(n), while calling a separate height function at every node is slower?
choices: It skips the leaves entirely
It uses a queue instead of recursion
Each subtree's height is computed once and reused by its parent
It only walks down the left spine of the tree
questions.explanation: check_height computes each subtree's height once, in postorder, and hands it to the parent. The naive version recomputes the heights of the same subtrees from scratch at every ancestor.

questions.question: Why do Java's TreeMap and C++'s std::map use self-balancing trees rather than plain BSTs?
questions.answer: A plain BST degenerates into a chain with O(n) operations when keys arrive in sorted order. Self-balancing trees (usually red-black trees here) rotate nodes on insert and delete to keep the height O(log n), so every operation stays O(log n).
questions.explanation: Self-balancing trees trade a little extra work per update for a guaranteed logarithmic height.

questions.question: Match each problem with the approach that fits it.

pairs.left: Return the values seen from the right side
pairs.right: BFS, keeping the last node of each level

pairs.left: Is this tree a mirror image of itself?
pairs.right: Recursion comparing two nodes at a time

pairs.left: Find the 2nd smallest value in a BST
pairs.right: Inorder traversal, stopping at the 2nd value
Preorder DFS carrying the path so far

questions.explanation: Right side view is a level question, symmetry compares pairs of nodes, kth smallest in a BST is inorder, and root-to-leaf paths carry state downward in preorder.

questions.question: The diameter of a binary tree is the longest path between any two nodes, counted in edges. Which approach is O(n)?
choices: For every node, compute both subtree heights from scratch
BFS from the root, returning the number of levels
Inorder traversal, measuring from the first value to the last
One postorder pass returning heights and updating a best total of left plus right height
questions.explanation: The longest path through a node uses its left height plus its right height. One postorder pass can return heights upward while updating a best-so-far value. Recomputing heights at every node repeats work, and the path does not have to pass through the root.

questions.question: Which inputs are worth testing for almost any tree function? Select all that apply.
choices: An empty tree
A single node
A chain where every node has only one child
A tree with exactly one million nodes
A tree whose values are all prime
questions.explanation: An empty tree checks the base case, a single node checks leaf handling, and a lopsided chain makes one child missing at every node. Huge trees and special values rarely reveal logic bugs.
